entries.title: The Mamluk Sultanate
entries.summary: The Mamluks were a military slave-origin elite who ruled Egypt and Syria from 1250 to 1517, defeating the Mongols at Ayn Jalut and later falling to the Ottomans.
entries.detailed_information: Mamluk officers took power from the Ayyubids in Egypt. They halted Mongol expansion at Ayn Jalut (1260) and dismantled remaining Crusader footholds over time. Cairo flourished as a political, commercial, and scholarly center; a ceremonial Abbasid caliphate was hosted there after Baghdad's fall. In 1517, Ottoman Sultan Selim I defeated the Mamluks and incorporated Egypt into the Ottoman Empire.
entries.historical_significance: Defenders against Mongols and Crusaders; major late medieval Islamic power.
related_questions: How did the Ottomans conquer Egypt?

entries.title: Battle of Ayn Jalut
entries.summary: At Ayn Jalut in 1260 CE, Mamluk forces defeated a Mongol army, stopping Mongol advance into Egypt and marking a major turning point in regional history.
entries.detailed_information: Following the Mongol sack of Baghdad (1258) and pressure on Syria, the Mamluks under Qutuz (with Baybars playing a major role in many accounts) won at Ayn Jalut in Palestine. The victory preserved Egypt as a Muslim stronghold and reshaped Near Eastern politics.
entries.historical_significance: First major permanent check on Mongol expansion in the Levant/Egypt theater.
